chapter.title: The fire spreads: France falls, Britain holds

cards.body:
The fire did not burn the French house slowly from the front, where everyone stood with hoses. It found the one back door nobody was watching, rushed through, and the house was full of smoke before the hoses turned around.

Then it reached the gap between houses: about 33 km of open water. Fire cannot cross water. All it could do was throw sparks over from the air, and the next house had people on the roof swatting them out.

cards.title: One punch at the unguarded door
cards.body:
In May 1940 France and Britain together had about as many soldiers and tanks as Germany. On paper it was an even fight. France also had the Maginot Line, a chain of concrete forts along its border with Germany.

Germany did not attack the forts. On 10 May 1940 it marched into the Netherlands and Belgium to the north. The best French and British armies rushed north to meet them, exactly as the Germans hoped.

The main German tank force went somewhere else: through the Ardennes, a hilly forest in southern Belgium that French planners thought too thick for tanks. It crossed the river Meuse near Sedan on 13 May and then drove west, toward the sea.

The tanks did not stop to clear each town. Dive-bombers flew ahead and broke up whatever stood in the road. By 20 May the tanks reached the Channel coast. The armies that had rushed north were now cut off from the rest of France.

This way of fighting is often called Blitzkrieg, a German word meaning lightning war: tanks, planes and radios used together to move faster than the enemy can react. French orders went by messenger and telephone, and by the time they arrived the situation they described was gone.

cards.prompt: France and Britain had about as many tanks as Germany. So what beat them in May 1940?

options.text: Germany had secretly built far more tanks than anyone knew.
Germany packed its tanks into one fast punch through a spot France had left unguarded, and moved faster than French orders could follow.
The French army refused to fight.

whyNot.a: That's the old myth, not what happened: the numbers were about even. The difference was how the tanks were used, not how many there were.
whyNot.c: That's the story told afterwards, not the battle: French soldiers fought hard. The trouble was they were sent north while the real blow came through the Ardennes.

cards.reteach: Picture two boxers of equal weight. One spreads his strength along a wall of forts and up north where he expects the blow. The other puts everything into one fist and swings it at the gap. Speed and where you hit matter more than size.

cards.title: Dunkirk, and six weeks
cards.body:
The trapped British and French troops fell back to the port of Dunkirk. From 26 May to 4 June 1940, warships and hundreds of small boats carried about 338,000 soldiers across the Channel to England. Nearly all their tanks, trucks and guns were left on the beach.

Britain kept its soldiers but had to arm them again from nothing. Paris fell on 14 June. France signed an armistice, an agreement to stop fighting, on 22 June. From first shot to surrender: six weeks.

cards.title: Why the trick stopped at the water
cards.body:
Hitler's method needed tanks on the ground. Between France and England lies the Channel, about 33 km wide at its narrowest. Tanks cannot drive across water, and Britain's navy was far larger than Germany's. To land an army, Germany first had to clear the sky so its slow invasion boats would not be bombed.

So the summer of 1940 was fought in the air. From July to October German planes attacked British airfields, then cities. This is the Battle of Britain. Britain had two helps. One was radar, a new system that spotted incoming planes with radio waves, so fighters took off only when needed instead of patrolling until they ran out of fuel. The other was simple: a British pilot shot down over Britain could fly again the next day. A German pilot shot down became a prisoner.

In early September Germany switched from bombing airfields to bombing London. On 17 September 1940 Hitler put off the invasion. He never came back to it. The fire had reached a gap it could not jump.

cards.prompt: It is August 1940. A German general says: "We beat France in six weeks. We will do England the same way." What is he missing?

options.text: Britain's army on land is much bigger than France's was.
His method needs ground under the tanks. The Channel and the Royal Navy stop the tanks, and the Royal Air Force stops the planes meant to clear the way.
Britain has a Maginot Line of its own.

whyNot.a: That's the opposite of the situation: Britain's army had just left its weapons at Dunkirk. Its strength was at sea and in the air, not on land.
whyNot.c: That's France's wall, not Britain's: the Maginot Line sat on the French-German border, and the Germans simply drove round it.

cards.reteach: The thing that beat France was fast tanks on a road. Take away the road and the trick has nothing to run on. Water plus a big navy took away the road; radar plus fighters took away the air cover that might have replaced it.

cards.body:
People say "France had a weak army" or "the French just gave up". Spot it whenever someone explains the defeat by numbers or by courage.

The French army was large and mostly fought. It lost because its plan and its speed of command were built for the last war, and the Germans bet everything on one fast move through the one place France had not guarded.

cards.prompt: In one line: why did France fall and Britain not?

options.text: France was outnumbered; Britain was not.
Germany's fast tank punch worked on land in France, but it needed ground, and water plus air defence took that ground away in Britain.
France fought alone; Britain had America's help in 1940.

whyNot.a: That's the numbers myth again: in France the sides were about even. The Ardennes gap and speed decided it, not headcount.
whyNot.c: That's 1941, not 1940: America joined the war after December 1941, which is chapter 4. In 1940 Britain held with its own navy and air force.

cards.reteach: Same fire, two houses. The French house had an unlocked back door and the fire rushed through it in six weeks. The British house sat across 33 km of water, so the fire could only throw sparks from the air, and the sparks were put out.

cards.body: Open a map app. Measure Sedan to Calais: roughly what German tanks covered in about a week. Then measure Calais to Dover. That short strip of blue is the whole difference between the two halves of this chapter.

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now explain how an evenly matched France lost in six weeks, and why the same method could not cross the Channel to Britain.
